claims.text: The initial Al–Mg-based alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable single-phase solid solution produced by high-pressure–high-temperature synthesis.
Reported Mg-containing Al alloys have a tendency to contain or compete thermodynamically with intermetallic compounds.
Elevated temperature promotes long-range atomic diffusion in the Al–Mg-based alloy.
Temperatures from approximately 950 K to 1200 K are representative of the alloy's high-temperature service conditions.
At or above approximately 950 K, atomic mobility triggers decomposition of the metastable solid solution.
Thermal aging causes diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth of fine Mg-containing intermetallic precipitates from the metastable matrix.
The transformation pathway is governed by competing rates of intermetallic nucleation and growth versus retention of the solid solution.
Prolonged aging causes the intermetallic precipitates to coarsen and potentially segregate.
A fine, uniformly distributed intermetallic dispersion helps maintain a chemically homogeneous matrix.
Fine precipitates act as diffusion barriers and stabilize local chemistry.
A fine intermetallic dispersion permits formation of continuous protective Al2O3 and MgO layers.
A fine, uniform intermetallic dispersion retains high-temperature oxidation and corrosion resistance.
Coarse or segregated intermetallic phases locally deplete protective-scale-forming elements such as Al.
Coarse or segregated intermetallic phases disrupt protective oxide-scale continuity and adherence.
Coarsening or segregation produces a measurable loss of oxidation and corrosion resistance relative to the initial state.
Conditions below the proposed temperature and exposure-time thresholds retain the initial metastable state.
An as-synthesized specimen and a thermally aged specimen from the same alloy provide the controlled comparison.
Intermetallic phase size and distribution, electrochemical corrosion response, oxidation mass gain, and oxide-scale morphology and adherence are measurable outcomes of the comparison.

The hypothesis is falsified if aging produces no significant intermetallic formation or coarsening, or if intermetallic morphology changes do not correlate with measurable corrosion or oxidation changes.
